long_what_lies_beneath_the_distinct_pigm.title: What Lies Beneath the Distinct Pigmentation of Orcinus orca?

scenes.label: Astonishing Size
scenes.line: Large male orcas can reach a weight of over 10 t and grow to 10 m long. What are the true origins and hidden behaviours of this apex predator known as the orca?
scenes.image_prompt: A vast open ocean surface with calm water under an overcast sky., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Scientific Classification
scenes.line: The orca is a toothed whale and the largest member of the oceanic dolphin family. It is recognizable by its distinct pigmentation, being mostly black on top, white on the bottom, and having recognizable white eye patches.
scenes.image_prompt: Deep blue sea water viewed from a low angle., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Global Habitat
scenes.line: A cosmopolitan species, it inhabits a wide range of marine environments, from Arctic to Antarctic regions to tropical seas. Centuries ago, Basque sailors called them asesina ballena, meaning whale killer.
scenes.image_prompt: Cold polar sea water meeting distant icy horizons., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Latin Origins
scenes.line: Ancient Romans originally used orca for these animals, possibly borrowing Ancient Greek oryx. Conrad Gessner wrote the first scientific description of an orca in his 1558 publication.
scenes.image_prompt: A rocky coastline next to a deep blue sea., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Linnaeus Cataloging
scenes.line: Orcinus orca is one of many species originally described by Carl Linnaeus in his 1758 edition of Systema Naturae. The orca is one of 35 species in the oceanic dolphin family, which first appeared about 11 million years ago.
scenes.image_prompt: A quiet library desk with old paper sheets., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Skeleton Structure
scenes.line: The skeleton of the orca is typical for an oceanic dolphin, but more robust. The mean body temperature of the orca is 36 to 38 °C.
scenes.image_prompt: Museum exhibit space with a large marine mammal skeleton., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Insulating Layer
scenes.line: Like most marine mammals, orcas have a layer of insulating blubber ranging from 7.6 to 10 cm thick beneath the skin. The pulse is about 60 heartbeats per minute when the orca is at the surface, dropping to 30 beats per minute when submerged.
scenes.image_prompt: Ocean waves washing against a rocky shore., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Distinctive Fins
scenes.line: Orca pectoral fins are large and rounded, resembling paddles, with those of males significantly larger than those of females. Dorsal fins also exhibit sexual dimorphism, with those of males about 1.8 m high.
scenes.image_prompt: Coastal waters with gentle ripples reflecting the daylight., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Powerful Jaws
scenes.line: The orca's teeth are very strong, and its jaws exert a powerful grip. Orcas have good eyesight above and below the water, excellent hearing, and a good sense of touch.
scenes.image_prompt: Close up of smooth grey ocean stones under water., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Echolocation Abilities
scenes.line: They have exceptionally sophisticated echolocation abilities, detecting the location and characteristics of prey by emitting clicks. An individual orca can often be identified from its dorsal fin and saddle patch.
scenes.image_prompt: Sunlight beams shining down into deep blue ocean water., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Photographic Cataloging
scenes.line: Published directories contain identifying photographs and names for hundreds of North Pacific animals. Orcas are found in all oceans and most seas.
scenes.image_prompt: A collection of photographs laid out flat on a wooden table., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Population Numbers
scenes.line: Worldwide population estimates are uncertain, but recent consensus suggests a minimum of 50,000 in 2006. Orcas are apex predators, meaning that they themselves have no natural predators.
scenes.image_prompt: Open ocean waves moving steadily across the deep sea., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Daily Consumption
scenes.line: On average, an orca eats 227 kilograms each day. Some populations in the Norwegian and Greenland sea specialize in herring and follow that fish's autumnal migration.
scenes.image_prompt: Submerged view of open pelagic waters., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Carousel Feeding
scenes.line: The orcas force the herring into a tight ball by releasing bursts of bubbles or flashing their white undersides. They then slap the ball with their tail flukes, stunning or killing up to 15 fish at a time.
scenes.image_prompt: Bubbles rising upward through clear blue ocean water., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Salmon Specialization
scenes.line: Salmon account for 96% of northeast Pacific residents' diet, particularly Chinook salmon. In New Zealand, sharks and rays appear to be important prey, including eagle rays and smooth hammerheads.
scenes.image_prompt: A clear river flowing over smooth rounded stones., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Great White Target
scenes.line: Orcas have preyed on broadnose sevengill sharks, whale sharks, and even great white sharks. Orcas target shark livers by flipping the sharks onto their backs, inducing a paralysis called tonic immobility.
scenes.image_prompt: Deep blue ocean water viewed from beneath the surface., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Shark Avoidance
scenes.line: The arrival of an orca in an area can cause white sharks to flee and forage elsewhere. Orcas are sophisticated and effective predators of marine mammals, including dolphins and porpoises.
scenes.image_prompt: An empty expanse of open blue sea., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Exhaustion Chases
scenes.line: While hunting these species, orcas usually have to chase them to exhaustion. For highly social species, orca pods try to separate an individual from its group.
scenes.image_prompt: Choppy ocean surface with white foam on the waves., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Ice Environment Tactics
scenes.line: Arctic orcas may attack beluga whales and narwhals stuck in pools enclosed by sea ice. By contrast, orcas appear to be wary of pilot whales, which have been recorded to mob and chase them.
scenes.image_prompt: Floating chunks of sea white ice in cold polar water., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Large Whale Targets
scenes.line: Orcas also prey on larger species such as sperm whales, grey whales, humpback whales and minke whales. On three occasions in 2019, orcas were recorded to have killed blue whales off the south coast of Western Australia.
scenes.image_prompt: Massive deep blue ocean swells under an open sky., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Massive Prey Size
scenes.line: Among them was an individual measuring 18 to 22 metres. Large whales require much effort and coordination to kill and orcas often target calves.
scenes.image_prompt: Vast open sea stretching out to a distant horizon., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Tooth Rake Marks
scenes.line: Large whales often show signs of orca attack via tooth rake marks. Pods of female sperm whales sometimes protect themselves by forming a protective circle around their calves.
scenes.image_prompt: Clear sea water viewed from a low coastal vantage point., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Humpback Intervention
scenes.line: There is also evidence that humpback whales will defend against or mob orcas who are attacking. Orcas have been revered by indigenous peoples from regions including the Pacific Northwest, Australia and Peru.
scenes.image_prompt: Ocean surface disturbed by rolling waves., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Western Fear
scenes.line: Western cultures have historically feared them. They have been taken by whalers when stocks of larger species have declined.
scenes.image_prompt: Dark grey ocean waters under a heavy stormy sky., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Captivity Era
scenes.line: Since the 1960s, orcas have been trained to perform in marine parks, a practice that has been criticized as unethical. Orcas rarely pose a threat to humans, and no fatal attack has been recorded in the wild.
scenes.image_prompt: Concrete pool architecture under bright outdoor daylight., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Captive Incidents
scenes.line: However, captive orcas have injured or killed their handlers in marine theme parks. Prior to the advent of industrial whaling, great whales may have been the major food source for orcas.
scenes.image_prompt: An indoor aquatic facility with large glass viewing panels., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Exploding Harpoons
scenes.line: The introduction of modern whaling techniques may have aided orcas by the sound of exploding harpoons indicating the availability of prey to scavenge. Compressed air inflation of whale carcasses caused them to float, thus exposing them to scavenging.
scenes.image_prompt: A rusty harpoon gun on the deck of a vessel looking out at the ocean., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Devastation of Whales
scenes.line: However, the devastation of great whale populations by unfettered whaling has possibly reduced their availability for orcas. This caused them to expand their consumption of smaller marine mammals, thus contributing to the decline of these as well.
scenes.image_prompt: Open ocean with gentle waves under an overcast sky., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Disabling Prey
scenes.line: Often, to avoid injury, orcas disable their prey before killing and eating it. This may involve throwing it in the air, slapping it with their tails, ramming it, or breaching and landing on it.
scenes.image_prompt: Turbulent ocean water with splashes near a rocky coastline., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Shallow Water Beaching
scenes.line: In steeply banked beaches off Península Valdés, Argentina, and the Crozet Islands, orcas feed on South American sea lions and southern elephant seals in shallow water. They even beach temporarily to grab prey before wriggling back to the sea.
scenes.image_prompt: A steeply sloped pebble beach meeting the ocean., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Learned Behavior
scenes.line: Beaching, usually fatal to cetaceans, is not an instinctive behaviour, and can require years of practice for the young. Orcas can then release the animal near juvenile whales, allowing the younger whales to practice the difficult capture technique on the now-weakened prey.
scenes.image_prompt: A coastline with smooth rounded rocks and shallow clear water., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Antarctic Wave Hunting
scenes.line: In the Antarctic, type B orcas hunt Weddell seals and other prey by wave hunting. They spy hop to locate them resting on ice floes, and then swim in groups to create waves that wash over the floe.
scenes.image_prompt: Cold polar waters with floating chunks of white ice., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Aleutian Sea Otters
scenes.line: In the Aleutian Islands, a decline in sea otter populations in the 1990s was controversially attributed by some scientists to orca predation, although with no direct evidence. Orcas have been observed preying on terrestrial mammals, such as moose swimming between islands off the northwest coast of North America.
scenes.image_prompt: Rocky islands and cold waters in a remote northern bay., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Cannibalism Evidence
scenes.line: Orca cannibalism has also been reported based on analysis of stomach contents, but this is likely to be the result of scavenging remains dumped by whalers. One orca was also attacked by its companions after being shot.
scenes.image_prompt: A wooden dock by the ocean with old rusty chains., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Transient Ecotypes
scenes.line: However, in a 2026 study, evidence was found that transient Bigg's orcas cannibalize resident orca individuals. It was also considered more appropriate to interpret the interactions between ecotypes as interspecies predation rather than cannibalism of fellows with the same ecological role.
scenes.image_prompt: Deep blue ocean water viewed from slightly above., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Harassing Porpoises
scenes.line: Although resident orcas have never been observed to eat other marine mammals, they occasionally harass and kill porpoises and seals for no apparent reason. Some dolphins recognize resident orcas as harmless and remain in the same area.
scenes.image_prompt: Calm coastal waters near a rocky headland., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Seabird Consumption
scenes.line: Orcas do consume seabirds but are more likely to kill and leave them uneaten. Penguin species recorded as prey in Antarctic and sub-Antarctic waters include gentoo penguins, chinstrap penguins, king penguins and rockhopper penguins.
scenes.image_prompt: Seabirds flying low over grey ocean waves., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Cormorants and Gulls
scenes.line: Orcas in many areas may prey on cormorants and gulls. A captive orca at Marineland of Canada discovered it could regurgitate fish onto the surface, attracting sea gulls, and then eat the birds.
scenes.image_prompt: Sea gulls resting on wooden pylons near the water., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Copying Behavior
scenes.line: Four others then learned to copy the behaviour. Day-to-day orca behaviour generally consists of foraging, travelling, resting and socializing.
scenes.image_prompt: Water surface ripples in a quiet aquatic enclosure., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Surface Activities
scenes.line: Orcas frequently engage in surface behaviour such as breaching jumping completely out of the water and tail-slapping. These activities may have a variety of purposes, such as courtship, communication, dislodging parasites, or play.
scenes.image_prompt: A splash of white water on a blue ocean surface., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Spyhopping Behavior
scenes.line: Spyhopping is a behaviour in which a whale holds its head above water to view its surroundings. They can also reach speeds of up to 15.5 m/s 56 km/h 35 mph.
scenes.image_prompt: Calm ocean water with a slight ripple., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Surplus Killing
scenes.line: Orcas will engage in surplus killing, that is, killing that is not designed to be for food. As an example, a BBC film crew witnessed orcas in British Columbia playing with a male Steller sea lion to exhaustion, but not eating it.
scenes.image_prompt: Choppy open ocean water under a grey sky., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Salmon Hats
scenes.line: Some orcas have been observed swimming with dead salmon on their heads, resembling hats. Orcas have complex societies.
scenes.image_prompt: Clear coastal ocean water near the surface., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Primate Comparison
scenes.line: Only elephants and higher primates live in comparably complex social structures. Due to orcas' complex social bonds, many marine experts have concerns about how humane it is to keep them in captivity.
scenes.image_prompt: Distant rocky islands shrouded in light mist., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Eastern North Pacific
scenes.line: Resident orcas in the eastern North Pacific live in particularly complex and stable social groups. Unlike any other known mammal social structure, resident whales of both sexes live with their mothers for their entire lives.
scenes.image_prompt: Pacific Northwest coastline with steep rocky cliffs., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Matriarch Families
scenes.line: These family groups are based on matrilines consisting of the eldest female matriarch and her sons and daughters, and the descendants of her daughters, etc. The average size of a matriline is 5.5 animals.
scenes.image_prompt: Quiet coastal inlet surrounded by evergreen forests., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Six Generations
scenes.line: Because females can reach age 90, as many as six generations may travel together. Individuals separate for only a few hours at a time, to mate or forage.
scenes.image_prompt: Open ocean waters under a vast horizon., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Luna Separation
scenes.line: The permanent separation of an individual from a resident matriline has only been recorded once, in the case of an orca named Luna. Closely related matrilines form loose aggregations called pods, usually consisting of one to four matrilines.
scenes.image_prompt: A narrow coastal channel with rocky shores., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Pod Separation
scenes.line: Unlike matrilines, pods may separate for weeks or months at a time. DNA testing indicates resident males nearly always mate with females from other pods.
scenes.image_prompt: Open ocean expanse under scattered clouds., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Clans Structure
scenes.line: Clans, the next level of resident social structure, are composed of pods with similar dialects, and common but older maternal heritage. The highest association layer is the community, which consists of pods that regularly associate with each other but share no maternal relations or dialects.
scenes.image_prompt: Coastal waters with gentle ripples on the surface., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Astonishing Sonar Discovery
scenes.line: Scientist Ken Balcomb has extensively studied orcas since 1976 and is the research biologist responsible for discovering US Navy sonar may harm orcas. He studied orcas from the Center for Whale Research, located in Friday Harbor, Washington.
scenes.image_prompt: a marine research station overlooking coastal waters with binoculars on a wooden railing, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Home Porch Observations
scenes.line: He was also able to study orcas from his home porch perched above Puget Sound, where the animals hunt and play in summer months. In May 2003, Balcomb along with other whale watchers near the Puget Sound coastline noticed uncharacteristic behaviour displayed by the orcas.
scenes.image_prompt: a wooden porch overlooking a calm ocean sound with forested islands in the distance, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Agitated Whales
scenes.line: The whales seemed agitated and were moving haphazardly, attempting to lift their heads free of the water to escape the sound of the sonars. Balcomb confirmed at the time that strange underwater pinging noises detected with underwater microphones were sonar.
scenes.image_prompt: orca whales surfacing together in choppy coastal water with misty mountains behind them, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Navy Frigate Source
scenes.line: The sound originated from a U.S. Navy frigate 12 miles distant, Balcomb said. Three years prior to Balcomb's discovery, research in the Bahamas showed 14 beaked whales washed up on the shore.
scenes.image_prompt: a grey naval ship sailing on the open ocean under an overcast grey sky, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Sonar Exercise Activation
scenes.line: These whales were beached on the day US Navy destroyers were activated into sonar exercise. Of the 14 whales beached, six of them died.
scenes.image_prompt: modern naval destroyers underway in a line formation on the blue ocean, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: CAT Scan Evidence
scenes.line: These six dead whales were studied, and CAT scans of two of the whale heads showed hemorrhaging around the brain and the ears. This hemorrhaging around the brain and the ears is consistent with decompression sickness.
scenes.image_prompt: medical laboratory interior with diagnostic computer screens showing grayscale brain scans, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Canadian Protection Decision
scenes.line: Another conservation concern was made public in September 2008 when the Canadian government decided it was not necessary to enforce further protections for orcas aside from the laws already in place. In response to this decision, six environmental groups sued the federal government.
scenes.image_prompt: government office building exterior with a flagpole flying a national flag, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Threats on Coast
scenes.line: The groups claimed orcas were facing threats along the British Columbia Coast including increased boat traffic, water toxic wastes, and low salmon population. The federal government did nothing to protect them.
scenes.image_prompt: commercial cargo ships and fishing boats navigating a narrow coastal strait, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Underwater Noise Concerns
scenes.line: Underwater noise from shipping, drilling, and other human activities is a significant concern in some key orca habitats, including Johnstone Strait and Haro Strait. In the mid-1990s, loud underwater noises from salmon farms were used to deter seals.
scenes.image_prompt: an industrial oil drilling platform operating out at sea on calm water, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Avoidance of Waters
scenes.line: Orcas also avoided the surrounding waters. High-intensity sonar used by the Navy disturbs orcas along with other marine mammals.
scenes.image_prompt: empty blue ocean water surface with gentle ripples and no animals present, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Whale Watching Stress
scenes.line: Orcas are popular with whale watchers, which may stress the whales and alter their behaviour, particularly if boats approach too closely or block their lines of travel. The Exxon Valdez oil spill adversely affected orcas in Prince William Sound and Alaska's Kenai Fjords region.
scenes.image_prompt: multiple small tourist boats crowding around marine wildlife on the water surface, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Disappearing Pod Members
scenes.line: Eleven members of one resident pod disappeared the following year. The spill damaged salmon and other prey populations, which in turn damaged local orcas.
scenes.image_prompt: a pod of black and white whales swimming in a straight line through dark water, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: AT1 Transient Population
scenes.line: By 2009, scientists estimated the AT1 transient population numbered only seven individuals and had not reproduced since the spill. This population is expected to die out.
scenes.image_prompt: a pair of orcas surfacing together near a steep fjord wall in Alaska, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: CITES Appendix II
scenes.line: Orcas are included in Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species, meaning international trade is regulated. The Haida regarded orcas as the most powerful animals in the ocean, and their mythology tells of orcas living in houses and towns under the sea.
scenes.image_prompt: a large official international document on a wooden desk with a fountain pen, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Submerged Human Form
scenes.line: According to these stories, they took on human form when submerged, and humans who drowned went to live with them. For the Kwakwaka'wakw, the orca was regarded as the ruler of the undersea world, with sea lions for slaves and dolphins for warriors.
scenes.image_prompt: sunlight filtering down through deep blue ocean water creating shimmering patterns, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Souls of Deceased Chiefs
scenes.line: In Nuu-chah-nulth and Kwakwaka'wakw mythology, orcas may embody the souls of deceased chiefs. The Tlingit of southeastern Alaska regarded the orca as custodian of the sea and a benefactor of humans.
scenes.image_prompt: an old wooden ceremonial mask resting on a woven cedar mat indoors, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Lummi Relations
scenes.line: The Lummi consider orca to be people, referring to them as qwe'lhol'mechen which means our relations under the waves. The Maritime Archaic people of Newfoundland also had great respect for orcas, as evidenced by stone carvings found in a 4,000-year-old burial at the Port au Choix Archaeological Site.
scenes.image_prompt: indigenous people standing on a wooden pier looking out over calm coastal waters, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Siberian Yupik Wolves
scenes.line: In the tales and beliefs of the Siberian Yupik people, orcas are said to appear as wolves in winter, and wolves as orcas in summer. The Ainu people of Hokkaido, the Kuril Islands, and southern Sakhalin often referred to orcas in their folklore and myth as Repun Kamuy to bring fortunes to the coasts.
scenes.image_prompt: snow-covered tundra landscape bordering an icy cold sea under a pale winter sun, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Pliny the Elder Description
scenes.line: The first written description of an orca was given by Pliny the Elder circa AD 70. Pliny wrote that orcas are an enormous mass of savage flesh with teeth and are the enemy of other kinds of whale.
scenes.image_prompt: an old leather-bound manuscript book opened to a page of Latin text on a wooden table, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Attacks on Ice Floes
scenes.line: In one instance, orcas tried to tip ice floes on which a dog team and photographer of the Terra Nova Expedition were standing. In the 1970s, a surfer in California was bitten, but the orca then retreated.
scenes.image_prompt: large flat chunks of floating sea ice drifting in cold polar waters, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Alaska Boy Bumped
scenes.line: In 2005, a boy in Alaska who was splashing in a region frequented by harbour seals was bumped by an orca that apparently misidentified him as prey. Beginning around 2020, one or more pods of orcas began to attack sailing vessels off the southern tip of Europe, and a few were sunk.
scenes.image_prompt: shallow coastal water splashing against rocky shorelines in an Alaskan bay, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Iberian Coast Interactions
scenes.line: At least 15 interactions between orcas and boats off the Iberian coast were reported in 2020. According to the Atlantic Orca Working Group as many as 500 vessels have been damaged between 2020 and 2023.
scenes.image_prompt: coastal waters near the Strait of Gibraltar with distant cargo ships on the horizon, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Catamaran Rudder Damage
scenes.line: In one video, an orca can be seen biting on one of the two rudders ripped from a catamaran near Gibraltar. The captain of the vessel reported this was the second attack on a vessel under his command and the orcas focused on the rudders.
scenes.image_prompt: the stern of a damaged catamaran showing missing rudder fittings in blue water, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Norway Ramming Incident
scenes.line: After an orca repeatedly rammed a vessel off the coast of Norway in 2023, there is a concern the behaviour is spreading to other areas. This has led to recommendations that sailors now carry bags of sand to drop into the water near the rudder, which is thought to confuse the sonar signal.
scenes.image_prompt: a steep Norwegian fjord wall plunging straight down into deep dark coastal water, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Expert Divisions
scenes.line: Experts were divided as to whether the behaviour was some sort of revenge or protection response to a previous traumatic incident, or playful or frustrated attempts to get a boat's propeller to emit a stream of high-speed water. Unlike wild orcas, captive orcas have made nearly two dozen attacks on humans since the 1970s, some of which have been fatal.
scenes.image_prompt: marine scientists having a discussion around a table covered in nautical charts, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Fishermen Competition
scenes.line: Competition with fishermen also led to orcas being regarded as pests.
scenes.image_prompt: commercial fishing vessel with nets and winch equipment on deck, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

long_what_is_the_true_size_of_the_giant_.title: What is the True Size of the Giant Squid Architeuthis dux in the Abyssal Depths?

scenes.label: Astonishing Giant Squid
scenes.line: The giant squid known as Architeuthis dux is a species of deep-ocean dwelling squid in the family Architeuthidae. What are the true dimensions and hidden behaviors of this elusive creature residing in the deep oceans?
scenes.image_prompt: dark ocean water surface, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Abyssal Gigantism
scenes.line: It can grow to a tremendous size, offering an example of abyssal gigantism in the ocean depths. Recent estimates put the maximum body size at around 5 m for females, with males slightly shorter.
scenes.image_prompt: vast dark ocean floor, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Colossal Squid Comparison
scenes.line: This makes it longer than the colossal squid at an estimated 4.2 m, but substantially lighter overall. The arms and tentacles make up much of the length while the mantle is about 2 m long.
scenes.image_prompt: two large marine animals, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Feeding Tentacles
scenes.line: The feeding tentacles of the giant squid, concealed in life, reach a length of 10 m. Claims of specimens measuring 20 m or more have not been scientifically documented by researchers.
scenes.image_prompt: coiled tentacles underwater, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Genetic Research
scenes.line: The number of different giant squid species has been debated, but genetic research suggests that only one species exists. In 2004, a Japanese research team obtained the first images of a living specimen in its habitat.
scenes.image_prompt: laboratory microscope on table, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Closest Relatives
scenes.line: The closest relatives are thought to be the four obscure species of neosquid in the family Neoteuthidae. Together, both families comprise the superfamily Architeuthoidea in biological classification systems.
scenes.image_prompt: marine specimens in jars, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Global Distribution
scenes.line: The giant squid is widespread, occurring in all of the world's oceans across multiple regions. It is usually found near continental and island slopes from the North Atlantic Ocean.
scenes.image_prompt: globe showing ocean currents, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Specific Regions
scenes.line: Specimens appear especially near Newfoundland, Norway, the northern British Isles, Spain, the Azores, and Madeira. Other locations include the South Atlantic around southern Africa and the North Pacific around Japan.
scenes.image_prompt: coastal cliffs and dark sea, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Tropical Rarity
scenes.line: Specimens are rare in tropical and polar latitudes across the globe. The vertical distribution of giant squid is incompletely known by marine scientists today.
scenes.image_prompt: polar ice and dark water, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Depth Range
scenes.line: Data from trawled specimens and sperm whale diving behavior suggest a range of 300 to 1,000 m depths. Like all squid, a giant squid has a mantle, eight arms, and two longer tentacles.
scenes.image_prompt: deep sea diving submersible, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Unique Length
scenes.line: The tentacles are the longest known tentacles of any cephalopod species in the ocean. Scientifically documented specimens have masses of hundreds, rather than thousands, of kilograms.
scenes.image_prompt: long squid tentacles floating, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Suction Cups
scenes.line: The inside surfaces are lined with hundreds of subspherical suction cups on stalks. Each suction cup measures 2 to 5 cm in diameter.
scenes.image_prompt: close up of suction cups, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Serrated Rings
scenes.line: The circumference of these suckers is lined with sharp, finely serrated rings of chitin. The perforation of these teeth and suction serve to attach the squid to its prey.
scenes.image_prompt: microscopic view of jagged edge, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Whale Scars
scenes.line: It is common to find circular scars from suckers on or close to the head of sperm whales. Each tentacular club is divided into three regions named carpus, manus, and dactylus.
scenes.image_prompt: scarred skin of a whale, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Carpus Region
scenes.line: The carpus has a dense cluster of cups arranged in six or seven irregular rows. The manus is broader closer to the end, featuring enlarged suckers in two medial rows.
scenes.image_prompt: clustered small circles, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Dactylus Tip
scenes.line: The dactylus forms the final tip of the tentacular club structure. The bases of all arms and tentacles surround the animal's single, parrot-like beak.
scenes.image_prompt: tapered tentacle end, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Rear Fins
scenes.line: Giant squid have small fins at the rear of their mantles used for locomotion. They move through jet propulsion by pushing water through the siphon in rhythmic pulses.
scenes.image_prompt: small fins on a mantle, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Quick Movement
scenes.line: They move quickly by expanding the cavity and contracting muscles to jet water through the siphon. Giant squid breathe using two large gills inside the mantle cavity.
scenes.image_prompt: fast moving dark shape, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Closed Circulation
scenes.line: The circulatory system is closed, which is a distinct characteristic of cephalopods. Like other squid, they contain dark ink within their bodies.
scenes.image_prompt: complex vascular network, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Nervous System
scenes.line: The giant squid has a sophisticated nervous system and complex brain attracting scientific interest. It has the largest eyes of any living creature except perhaps the colossal squid.
scenes.image_prompt: neural pathway graphic, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Eye Dimensions
scenes.line: The eyes measure up to at least 27 cm in diameter with a 9 cm pupil. Only the extinct ichthyosaurs are known to have had larger eyes than these.
scenes.image_prompt: measured circular lens, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Light Detection
scenes.line: Large eyes can better detect light, including scarce bioluminescent light in deep water. The giant squid probably cannot see color, but can discern small differences in tone.
scenes.image_prompt: glowing bioluminescent specks, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Neutral Buoyancy
scenes.line: They maintain neutral buoyancy through an ammonium chloride solution found throughout their bodies. This fluid is lighter than seawater and differs from the gas-filled swim bladder of fish.
scenes.image_prompt: chemical liquid in a beaker, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Taste and Consumption
scenes.line: The solution tastes somewhat like salty liquorice and makes consumption unappealing to humans. Giant squid use organs called statocysts to sense their orientation and motion in water.
scenes.image_prompt: herb and spice roots on table, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Age Determination
scenes.line: The age can be determined by growth rings in the statocyst statolith like tree rings. Much of their age is known from estimated growth rings and undigested beaks in sperm whale stomachs.
scenes.image_prompt: microscopic rings in a shell, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Juvenile in Toyama
scenes.line: Another juvenile, approximately 3.7 metres long, was encountered and filmed alive in the harbour in the Japanese city of Toyama on 24 December 2015. After being filmed and viewed by a large number of spectators, it was guided out of the harbour into Toyama Bay by a diver.
scenes.image_prompt: An underwater view of a harbor with clear water., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Mitochondrial DNA
scenes.line: Analysis of the mitochondrial DNA of giant squid individuals from all over the world has found little variation between individuals across the globe. Only 181 genetic base pairs out of 20,331 differed among the global samples.
scenes.image_prompt: A scientific laboratory with equipment analyzing genetic data on a screen., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Single species
scenes.line: This suggests that there is only a single species of giant squid in the world. Squid larvae may be dispersed by ocean currents across vast distances.
scenes.image_prompt: A vast open ocean stretching toward the horizon under a cloudy sky., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Prey types
scenes.line: Recent studies have shown giant squid feed on deep-sea fish, such as the orange roughy, and other squid species. They catch prey using the two tentacles, gripping it with serrated sucker rings on the ends.
scenes.image_prompt: Deep sea fish swimming near rocky ocean floor formations., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Beak and radula
scenes.line: Then they bring it toward the powerful beak, and shred it with the radula before it reaches the esophagus. They are believed to be solitary hunters, as only individual giant squid have been caught in fishing nets.
scenes.image_prompt: A sharp biological beak structure in a dark aquatic setting., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: New Zealand trawl
scenes.line: The majority of giant squid caught by trawl in New Zealand waters have been associated with the local hoki fishery. Hoki do not feature in the squid's diet.
scenes.image_prompt: A fishing trawler vessel on the open sea., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Prey overlap
scenes.line: This suggests giant squid and hoki prey on the same animals. The known predators of adult giant squid include sperm whales, pilot whales, southern sleeper sharks, and killer whales.
scenes.image_prompt: Deep sea creatures swimming near the dark ocean floor., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Juvenile predators
scenes.line: Juveniles may fall prey to other large deep sea predators. Giant squid have also been recently discovered to presumably steal food from each other.
scenes.image_prompt: Dark deep sea environment with shadows of large marine life., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Galicia stranding
scenes.line: In mid-to-late October 2016, a giant squid measuring 9 m long, including its tentacles, washed ashore in Galicia, Spain. The squid had been photographed alive by a tourist named Javier Ondicol shortly before its death.
scenes.image_prompt: A sandy beach shoreline with waves crashing gently., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: CEPESMA examination
scenes.line: Examination of its corpse by the Coordinators for the Study and Protection of Marine Species indicates it was attacked by another giant squid. It lost parts of its fins, received damage to its mantle and one of its gills, and lost an eye.
scenes.image_prompt: Marine researchers examining a large specimen on a shore., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Retreat to shallows
scenes.line: The intact nature of the specimen indicates that the giant squid managed to escape its rival by slowly retreating to shallow water. It died of its wounds in the shallow water.
scenes.image_prompt: Shallow coastal water gently lapping against a rocky shore., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Second Spanish document
scenes.line: The incident is the second to be documented among Architeuthis recorded in Spain, with the other occurring in Villaviciosa. Evidence in the form of stomach contents containing beak fragments from other giant squid in Tasmania also supports cannibalism.
scenes.image_prompt: A rocky coastal landscape with cliffs meeting the sea., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Prey competition
scenes.line: Alternatively, such squid-on-squid attacks may be a result of competition for prey. These traits are seen in the Humboldt squid as well, indicating cannibalism in large squid may be more common than thought.
scenes.image_prompt: Open ocean waters with deep shadows beneath the surface., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Population difficulty
scenes.line: Scientists have been unable to determine the worldwide population of giant squid to any degree of accuracy. Estimates have been put together based on the number of giant squid beaks found in the stomachs of deceased sperm whales.
scenes.image_prompt: A researcher looking out over an endless ocean expanse., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Annual consumption
scenes.line: Sperm whales consume between 4.3 and 131 million giant squid annually. This implies that the giant squid population is likewise well into the millions.
scenes.image_prompt: A sperm whale diving vertically into the dark ocean., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Taxonomy debate
scenes.line: The taxonomy of the giant squid, as with many cephalopod genera, has long been debated. Lumpers and splitters may propose as many as seventeen species or as few as one.
scenes.image_prompt: Old leather-bound books and scientific papers on a wooden desk., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Architeuthis dux
scenes.line: Among the broadest list of names is Architeuthis dux, the Atlantic giant squid. In March 2013, researchers at the University of Copenhagen suggested that based on DNA research there is only one species.
scenes.image_prompt: An old nautical chart spread out on a wooden table., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Aristotle description
scenes.line: Aristotle, who lived in the fourth century BC, described a large squid, which he called teuthus. Pliny the Elder, living in the first century AD, also described a gigantic squid in his Natural History.
scenes.image_prompt: An ancient stone archway overlooking the Mediterranean Sea., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Mariner tales
scenes.line: Tales of giant squid have been common among mariners since ancient times. These tales may have led to the Norse legend of the kraken, a tentacled sea monster as large as an island.
scenes.image_prompt: An old wooden sailing ship on a dark and stormy sea., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Sea monk suggestion
scenes.line: Japetus Steenstrup suggested a giant squid was the species described as a sea monk to the Danish king Christian III circa 1550. The historian Otto Latva pointed out that many old stories about sea monsters were not associated with giant squid until the late 19th century.
scenes.image_prompt: A historical castle overlooking a cold northern sea., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Pragmatic view
scenes.line: Seafarers did not perceive giant squid as monsters, but as sea animals that could be utilized in various ways. Steenstrup wrote a number of papers on giant squid in the 1850s and first used the term Architeuthis in 1857.
scenes.image_prompt: A historic coastal fishing village with small wooden boats., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Alecton corvette
scenes.line: A portion of a giant squid was secured by the French corvette Alecton in 1861. From 1870 to 1880, many squid were stranded on the shores of Newfoundland.
scenes.image_prompt: A 19th-century naval sailing vessel on open waters., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Thimble Tickle Bay
scenes.line: A specimen washed ashore in Thimble Tickle Bay, Newfoundland, on 2 November 1878. Its mantle was reported to be 6.1 m long, with one tentacle 10.7 m long, and estimated as weighing 0.9 tonnes.
scenes.image_prompt: A desolate northern bay with calm dark water and rocky shores., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Manure processing
scenes.line: Many of these specimens were not preserved, often being processed into manure or animal feed. In 1873, a squid attacked a dory near Bell Island, Newfoundland.
scenes.image_prompt: An old rustic farm landscape under a grey sky., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: New Zealand strandings
scenes.line: Many strandings also occurred in New Zealand during the late 19th century. It is not known why giant squid become stranded on shore, but it may be because deep, cold water distribution is altered.
scenes.image_prompt: A sandy beach in New Zealand meeting the ocean., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Cyclical belief
scenes.line: Many scientists who have studied squid mass strandings believe they are cyclical and predictable. Architeuthis specialist Frederick Aldrich proposed an interval of 90 years to correctly predict a relatively small stranding.
scenes.image_prompt: A tidal shoreline with receding water leaving wet sand patterns., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Giant squid caught
scenes.line: In 2004, another giant squid, later named Archie, was caught off the coast of the Falkland Islands by a fishing trawler. It was 8.62 m long and was sent to the Natural History Museum in London to be studied and preserved.
scenes.image_prompt: A large commercial fishing trawler operating on the ocean under daylight., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Public exhibition date
scenes.line: It was put on display on 1 March 2006 at the Darwin Centre. The find of such a large, complete specimen is very rare, as most specimens are in a poor condition.
scenes.image_prompt: Interior exhibition hall with modern display cases and architectural lighting., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Washed up dead
scenes.line: Most specimens have washed up dead on beaches or been retrieved from the stomachs of dead sperm whales. Researchers undertook a painstaking process to preserve the body.
scenes.image_prompt: Sperm whales swimming together in deep blue ocean water., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Transported on ice
scenes.line: It was transported to England on ice aboard a trawler, then defrosted, which took about four days. The major difficulty was that thawing the thick mantle took much longer than the tentacles.
scenes.image_prompt: Blocks of ice stacked neatly inside a refrigerated cargo hold., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Protecting the tentacles
scenes.line: To prevent the tentacles from rotting, scientists covered them in ice packs, and bathed the mantle in water. Then they injected the squid with a formol-saline solution to prevent rotting.
scenes.image_prompt: Scientists wearing protective gloves applying ice packs to marine specimens., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Glass tank display
scenes.line: It is now on show in a 9 m glass tank at the Darwin Centre of the Natural History Museum. In December 2005, the Melbourne Aquarium in Australia paid A$100,000 for the intact body of a 7-metre-long giant squid.
scenes.image_prompt: A tall glass aquarium tank filled with water inside a modern museum., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Block of ice
scenes.line: The giant squid was preserved in a giant block of ice, which had been caught by fishermen off the coast of New Zealand. The number of known giant squid specimens was close to 700 in 2011, and new ones are reported each year.
scenes.image_prompt: A massive block of clear ice sitting inside a large industrial freezer., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Museum exhibitions
scenes.line: Around 30 of these specimens are exhibited at museums and aquaria worldwide. The Museo del Calamar Gigante in Luarca, Spain, had by far the largest collection on public display.
scenes.image_prompt: Visitors walking through a dimly lit public museum gallery., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Storm damage
scenes.line: Many of the museum's specimens were destroyed during a storm in February 2014. The search for a live Architeuthis specimen includes attempts to find live young, including larvae.
scenes.image_prompt: Crashing ocean waves hitting a concrete sea wall during stormy weather., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Larval characteristics
scenes.line: The larvae closely resemble those of Nototodarus and Onykia, but are distinguished by the shape of the mantle attachment. By the turn of the 21st century, the giant squid remained one of the few extant megafauna to have never been photographed alive.
scenes.image_prompt: A laboratory microscope resting on a wooden desk next to sample slides., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Elusive natural history
scenes.line: Marine biologist and author Richard Ellis described it as the most elusive image in natural history. In 1993, an image purporting to show a diver with a live giant squid was published in the book European Seashells.
scenes.image_prompt: Open ocean waters reflecting a bright overcast sky from above., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Onykia robusta confusion
scenes.line: However, the animal in this photograph was a sick or dying Onykia robusta, not a giant squid. The first footage of live larval giant squid ever captured on film was in 2001.
scenes.image_prompt: A lone scuba diver swimming through deep blue oceanic water., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Discovery Channel broadcast
scenes.line: The footage was shown on Chasing Giants: On the Trail of the Giant Squid on the Discovery Channel. The first image of a live mature giant squid was taken on 15 January 2002, on Goshiki beach, Amino Cho, Kyoto Prefecture, Japan.
scenes.image_prompt: A television broadcast studio control room with multiple glowing monitors., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Surface discovery
scenes.line: The animal, which measured about 2 m in mantle length and 4 m in total length, was found near the water's surface. It was captured and tied to a quay, where it died overnight.
scenes.image_prompt: Calm coastal water surface reflecting the daylight sky., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: National Science Museum
scenes.line: The specimen was identified by Koutarou Tsuchiya of the Tokyo University of Fisheries and is on display at the National Science Museum of Japan. The first photographs of a live giant squid in its natural habitat were taken on 30 September 2004.
scenes.image_prompt: The facade of a large scientific museum building in Japan., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Teams collaboration
scenes.line: Tsunemi Kubodera and Kyoichi Mori had worked together for nearly two years to accomplish this. They used a five-ton fishing boat and only two crew members.
scenes.image_prompt: Two researchers working together on the deck of a research vessel., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Sperm whale ground
scenes.line: The images were created on their third trip to a known sperm whale hunting ground 970 km south of Tokyo. They had dropped a 900 m line baited with squid and shrimp, holding a camera and a flash.
scenes.image_prompt: Deep blue sea surface in a remote offshore location., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Attack on lure
scenes.line: After over twenty tries that day, an 8 m giant squid attacked the lure and snagged its tentacle. The camera took over 500 photos before the squid managed to break free after four hours, leaving its 5.5 m tentacle attached.
scenes.image_prompt: Underwater camera flash illuminating dark deep sea water., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: DNA test confirmation
scenes.line: Later DNA tests confirmed the animal as a giant squid. On 27 September 2005, Kubodera and Mori released the photographs to the world.
scenes.image_prompt: A scientist in a laboratory pipetting clear liquid into test tubes., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Ball of tentacles
